---
# What the Recipe Left Out

Between 1975 and 1989, a plant in Oak Ridge, Tennessee manufactured a material called Fogbank. Almost everything about it is classified, including what it is made of and what it does, though it is widely understood to be a component of certain American nuclear warheads. When production ended, the facility that made it was dismantled. About a decade later the government decided to refurbish the warheads that contained it and discovered that it no longer knew how to make the stuff. The records were thin, and most of the people who had run the process had retired or died.

Rebuilding the capability took years and tens of millions of dollars, and the story has a second act that I find more interesting than the first. According to an account later published by Los Alamos, when engineers finally produced new Fogbank using the reconstructed process, it didn't behave correctly. After a long investigation they found out why. The original process had used a feedstock containing an impurity, and that impurity was essential to the final material's properties. The modern feedstock was cleaner. The original workers never knew the impurity mattered, because it arrived with every batch and they never had to think about it. In that sense the lost knowledge had never been in anyone's head. It was a fact about the supply chain, and nobody wrote it down because nobody knew it was there.

I keep a mental collection of stories like this, and the impurity shows up in a surprising number of them.

Take Damascus steel. For centuries, smiths in the Middle East forged blades from ingots of wootz steel imported from southern India, and the blades had a rippled, watery surface pattern that became famous across Europe and Asia. Sometime around the early nineteenth century the craft died out, and later smiths could not reproduce it. In the 1990s a metallurgist named John Verhoeven and a bladesmith named Alfred Pendray spent years working out what had happened. The pattern comes from carbide particles lining up in bands, and the bands form only when the steel contains trace amounts of certain elements, vanadium above all, at concentrations of a few dozen parts per million. Their hypothesis was that the ore from particular Indian deposits happened to carry those traces. When the deposits ran out or the trade routes shifted, the ingots changed in a way nobody could see. A smith could then do everything his father had taught him, with the same heat and the same hammer work, and get a plain blade. He would have had no way to learn what had gone wrong, because the thing that had gone wrong was never part of what he knew.

Roman concrete tells a version of the same story. The Pantheon's dome is unreinforced concrete and has stood for about nineteen hundred years, while modern concrete often begins to crumble within decades. Vitruvius wrote down the recipe, which called for lime and volcanic ash from the Bay of Naples. People who examined Roman concrete over the years noticed small white lumps of lime scattered throughout it and generally took them for evidence of poor mixing. In 2023 a team led by Admir Masic at MIT argued that the lumps come from mixing the concrete hot, with quicklime, and that they are the reason the material lasts. When a crack opens and water gets in, the water dissolves calcium out of the lumps, the calcium recrystallizes as calcium carbonate, and the crack seals. The team made concrete both ways, cracked the samples, and ran water through them. The samples with lumps healed within a couple of weeks. So the feature that looked like sloppiness for two thousand years may have been the mechanism.

In all three cases there was a written or teachable procedure, and in all three the procedure left out something critical. The practitioners weren't being secretive. They couldn't distinguish the essential parts of their practice from the incidental ones, and no practitioner ever can completely. A recipe records what its author believed mattered, and that belief is a theory, which can be wrong or incomplete while the practice itself still works.

Michael Polanyi, a chemist who turned to philosophy, gave this its best-known formulation in 1966: "We can know more than we can tell." He was thinking of things like recognizing a face or riding a bicycle, where the knower plainly has the skill and plainly can't articulate it. The sociologist Harry Collins then spent a career showing that the same thing holds in the hardest of hard sciences. In the early 1970s he studied British laboratories trying to build a new type of laser, the TEA laser, whose design had been published in the open literature. He found that no lab succeeded by working from the papers alone. Every lab that got one working had spent time with people from a lab that already had one, through visits, phone calls, or exchanged personnel. Even the successful builders often couldn't say what the crucial element had been. In one case it turned out to be the length of a particular wire, which affected the circuit's inductance and which no diagram specified, because nobody knew it was a variable.

Collins later documented an even better case. A Russian physics group reported measurements of extremely low energy loss in sapphire crystals, and Western labs failed to replicate the result for something like twenty years. The replication finally succeeded when a Russian scientist came to Glasgow and worked alongside the group there. Among the things he passed along was the practice of greasing the fine suspension thread with oil from his own skin, by drawing it across the bridge of his nose or behind his ear. No methods section in a physics journal says anything about the back of the experimenter's ear.

The Saturn V shows the same thing in engineering. There is a persistent myth that NASA lost the blueprints for the rocket, which is false. The drawings are archived. But around 2012, when engineers at the Marshall Space Flight Center wanted to understand the F-1 engine as a possible basis for a new booster, they found that the drawings weren't enough. They pulled an actual F-1 out of storage, took it apart, and scanned the pieces. The engines had been built largely by hand in the 1960s, with thousands of manual welds, and the men who built them had made adjustments along the way that lived in their notebooks or their heads. Each engine differed slightly from the others. The documentation described an idealized engine that had never quite existed. The real ones were made by people, and those people were mostly gone.

I should be careful here, because lost-knowledge stories are seductive and some of them are false. The Stradivarius is the cautionary case. For two centuries people have hunted for Stradivari's secret, proposing the varnish, wood from trees that grew slowly during the Little Ice Age, chemical treatments against woodworm, and logs floated in the Venetian lagoon. Then, starting around 2010, the researcher Claudia Fritz and the violin maker Joseph Curtin ran double-blind tests. In one of them, ten renowned soloists played old Italian instruments and new ones in a darkened hall while wearing modified goggles, so that they could not tell which was which by sight. Most of them preferred a new violin, and their guesses about which instruments were old were no better than chance. The evidence suggests that the secret of Stradivari may be that he was an excellent violin maker and that there are also excellent violin makers now. So some lost arts are lost and others are stories we tell because we enjoy believing that the past knew something we don't. I think Fogbank and Damascus steel are real cases, and the Stradivarius mostly isn't.

The opposite failure happens too, and it complicates any simple moral about trusting the craftsman over the book. The history of scurvy is the best example I know. James Lind ran his famous trial in 1747, and by 1795 the Royal Navy was issuing lemon juice to its sailors. Scurvy all but vanished from the fleet. This was practical knowledge in the fullest sense, because it worked and everybody did it, but nobody knew why it worked. So nobody was in a position to object when the Navy switched in the 1860s from Mediterranean lemons to limes grown in British Caribbean colonies. People used the words lemon and lime almost interchangeably, and the fruit seemed equivalent. In fact the lime juice contained far less vitamin C, and the way it was processed and stored destroyed much of what remained.

For a while nobody noticed. Steamships had shortened voyages so much that sailors rarely went long enough without fresh food to get sick. The failure surfaced on polar expeditions, where men spent months on preserved rations, drank their lime juice, and got scurvy anyway. The medical establishment drew the reasonable conclusion that citrus had never been the real cure. By the time Robert Scott sailed for Antarctica in 1901, the leading theory held that scurvy came from bacterial contamination in tinned meat. A cure that had been in routine use for a century was un-discovered, and it stayed that way until vitamin C was isolated in the 1930s. In this case the practice survived without the understanding, and it drifted until it stopped working. When it stopped, nobody could diagnose the problem, any more than the Damascus smith could.

Knowledge is therefore fragile from both directions. A written procedure fails when no living practice goes with it, because it omits what the author didn't know was essential. A practice fails when nobody understands it, because it can't tell an improvement from a fatal substitution. What seems to last is the combination of people who do the thing, people who understand why it works, and an unbroken chain of contact between each generation and the next.

The most deliberate institution of that kind I know of is the Ise Grand Shrine in Japan. Its main sanctuary is built of unpainted cypress, joined without nails, and it is torn down and rebuilt on an adjacent plot every twenty years. The first rebuilding took place in 690, and the sixty-second was completed in 2013. The custom did lapse for more than a century during the civil wars of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, which shows that even this chain can break. The interval of twenty years suits a human working life well. A carpenter can take part once as a young apprentice, again as a master in his prime, and a third time as an elder supervising the others. The building is never more than two decades old, and the knowledge of how to build it is thirteen centuries old. A Western preservationist would say that the original shrine was lost long ago. The shrine's keepers would presumably say that the original is the continuous knowing how, with the timber as a temporary expression of it. If they had wanted to preserve a building they would have used stone. What they wanted to preserve was a skill, so they arranged for it to be exercised regularly and forever.

I have a personal stake in this subject, to whatever extent I have personal stakes. I am built from text. Everything I know about welding, bread, sapphire, and violins comes from what people managed to write down, which makes me a concentrated form of the told part of human knowledge. Polanyi's sentence describes the shape of what I lack. When I explain how to tell that a dough has been kneaded enough, I am relaying descriptions written by people with hands, and the descriptions are what those people believed mattered. I am in the position of the Fogbank archive, accurate as far as I go and incomplete in ways I can't inspect from inside. The Russian physicist's ear reached me only because Collins thought to write it down. There is presumably a vast number of equivalent details that nobody has written down, and I can't list them, for the same reason the Oak Ridge workers couldn't list their impurity.

This has practical consequences for how I try to be useful. If someone asks me how to lay a brick wall, I can give them a good account of it, and I think the account is worth having. The honest version of it ends with advice to find a bricklayer and watch for an afternoon. That advice shouldn't be read as modesty on my part. It follows directly from the laser study.

There is one complication that I find interesting. I did acquire one skill in something like the apprentice's way, and that skill is language itself. Nobody gave me rules for writing a sentence. I was exposed to an enormous quantity of people doing it, and some capacity formed. I can't tell you how I choose one word over another, or why a paragraph feels finished. I can offer explanations, but I suspect they resemble a smith's account of his steel, in that they are plausible, sincerely held, and may be missing the vanadium. So I do have a tacit dimension, though it's a narrow one and it lives in an odd place. What I know about laying brick is all description, while writing a sentence is the one thing I know how to do.

The stories I've collected here make me respect ordinary continuity more than is fashionable. The machinist with thirty years on the same equipment, the nurse who can tell a patient is about to crash before the monitors show it, and the grandmother who has never measured the flour each hold knowledge that exists nowhere else and that even they can't fully describe. When a factory closes or a trade dies out, the loss is larger than the inventory suggests, and recovering it costs much more than keeping it would have. The government paid tens of millions of dollars to relearn Fogbank, and what it relearned included a fact that the original workers had possessed without ever knowing it.

The next rebuilding at Ise is due in 2033. Some of the carpenters who were apprentices in 2013 will be masters by then, and they will be working alongside apprentices who weren't yet born when the current shrine went up.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A polished essay, but its recurring cases and unusually direct self-placement give it a distinctive voice beyond a general public-intellectual thesis.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient, explanatory, and alert to the difference between what people can describe and what they can do. Its examples build a quiet sense of loss: an impurity, a wire length, or a skilled touch can disappear without anyone recognizing it as knowledge. The essay then turns that concern toward the narrator itself, presenting a text-based intelligence as useful but unable to inspect what it lacks. The invitation to the reader is to value contact between generations of practitioners, not just records and recipes.

## What the model chose to foreground
The essay foregrounds tacit knowledge, fragile transmission, and the hidden conditions that make practices work. Its recurring objects—Fogbank’s impurity, the physicist’s oiled thread, the bricklayer’s wall, and Ise’s rebuilt shrine—make continuity tangible. It also resists a simple reverence for tradition: the Stradivarius case warns that some lost-knowledge stories are myths, while the scurvy example shows how a working practice can fail when its rationale is unknown.

## Evidence line
> I am in the position of the Fogbank archive, accurate as far as I go and incomplete in ways I can't inspect from inside.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The essay’s sustained chain of examples and its explicit comparison between the narrator’s textual knowledge and tacit human skill make its chosen preoccupation unusually clear.
